title: If I had…: the conditional
why: The third B1 lesson: the conditional (הָיִיתִי + present) and the two kinds of "if": the possible condition (אִם + future) and the imaginary one (לוּ + past). You reuse הָיִיתִי (unit 8) and the future (unit 9) to imagine and dream out loud.

{"lessons": ["

I would travel: הָיִיתִי + present

The Hebrew conditional is built from two pieces you already know: the past of \"to be\" (הָיִיתִי, הָיִיתָ…, unit 8) followed by the verb in the present. The first word changes with the person; the second agrees in gender and number, as always in the present. Think of it as Hebrew's \"would.\"

PersonHebrewPronunciation
I (man / woman)הָיִיתִי נוֹסֵעַ / הָיִיתִי נוֹסַעַתhayiti nose'a / hayiti nosa'at
you (man)הָיִיתָ נוֹסֵעַhayita nose'a
you (woman)הָיִית נוֹסַעַתhayit nosa'at
he / sheהוּא הָיָה נוֹסֵעַ / הִיא הָיְתָה נוֹסַעַתhu haya nose'a / hi hayta nosa'at
weהָיִינוּ נוֹסְעִיםhayinu nos'im
they (m. / f.)הֵם הָיוּ נוֹסְעִים / הֵן הָיוּ נוֹסְעוֹתhem hayu nos'im / hen hayu nos'ot

You already know the polite phrase הָיִיתִי רוֹצֶה (I would like): that's exactly this conditional!

Watch out: הָיִיתִי נוֹסֵעַ can also mean \"I used to go,\" just like English \"would\" in \"when I was a kid, I would go to the beach.\" Context decides; with an \"if,\" it's the conditional.

", "

Two kinds of \"if\"

If it's possible and it's about the future: אִם + future. English uses the present after \"if\" (\"if I have time\"); Hebrew happily uses the future, since it hasn't happened yet.

אִם יִהְיֶה לִי זְמַן, אֶלְמַד לְבַשֵּׁל.If I have time, I'll learn to cook. [im yihye li zman, elmad levashel]

יִהְיֶה (yihye) is the future of \"to be, there is.\" Like הָיָה לִי, it agrees with the thing you have: יִהְיֶה (m.), תִּהְיֶה (f.), יִהְיוּ (pl.). So: אִם תִּהְיֶה לִי חֻפְשָׁה (if I have a vacation).

If it's imaginary (it isn't true, you're dreaming): לוּ + past, then the conditional.

לוּ הָיָה לִי כֶּסֶף, הָיִיתִי קוֹנֶה בַּיִת בַּכְּפָר.If I had money, I would buy a house in the countryside. (a man speaking) [lu haya li kesef, hayiti kone bayit ba-kfar]

לוּ is a bit formal. In speech, Israelis very often say אִם for imaginary situations too: אִם הָיָה לִי כֶּסֶף, הָיִיתִי… It's the past followed by the conditional that shows you're dreaming.

", "

Dreaming out loud

To get the conversation going: מָה הָיִיתָ עוֹשֶׂה לוּ…? (to a man) / מָה הָיִית עוֹשָׂה לוּ…? (to a woman), \"what would you do if…?\".

מָה הָיִית עוֹשָׂה לוּ הָיְתָה לָךְ שָׁנָה שְׁלֵמָה בְּלִי עֲבוֹדָה?What would you do if you had a whole year without work? (to a woman) [ma hayit osa lu hayta lakh shana shlema bli avoda?]
הָיִיתִי מְטַיֶּלֶת בְּכָל הָעוֹלָם.I would travel all over the world. (a woman speaking) [hayiti metayelet be-khol ha-olam]

Two words for reacting: כְּדַאי (it's worth it) and חֲבָל (too bad). \"Too bad that…\" is חֲבָל שֶׁ…:

חֲבָל שֶׁאֵין לִי מְכוֹנִית!Too bad I don't have a car! [khaval she-ein li mekhonit!]

After \"too bad that,\" the sentence stays completely normal, just like in English. Good news: Hebrew has no special subjunctive forms to learn!
